<jats:p>
            We say an algorithm on
            <jats:italic>n</jats:italic>
            ×
            <jats:italic>n</jats:italic>
            matrices with integer entries in [−
            <jats:italic>M</jats:italic>
            ,
            <jats:italic>M</jats:italic>
            ] (or
            <jats:italic>n</jats:italic>
            -node graphs with edge weights from [−
            <jats:italic>M</jats:italic>
            ,
            <jats:italic>M</jats:italic>
            ]) is
            <jats:italic>truly subcubic</jats:italic>
            if it runs in
            <jats:italic>O</jats:italic>
            (
            <jats:italic>n</jats:italic>
            <jats:sup>3 − δ</jats:sup>
            ċ poly(log
            <jats:italic>M</jats:italic>
            )) time for some δ > 0. We define a notion of
            <jats:italic>subcubic reducibility</jats:italic>
            and show that many important problems on graphs and matrices solvable in
            <jats:italic>O</jats:italic>
            (
            <jats:italic>n</jats:italic>
            <jats:sup>3</jats:sup>
            ) time are
            <jats:italic>equivalent</jats:italic>
            under subcubic reductions. Namely, the following weighted problems either
            <jats:italic>all</jats:italic>
            have truly subcubic algorithms, or none of them do:
          </jats:p>
          <jats:p>•The all-pairs shortest paths problem on weighted digraphs (APSP).</jats:p>
          <jats:p>•Detecting if a weighted graph has a triangle of negative total edge weight.</jats:p>
          <jats:p>
            •Listing up to
            <jats:italic>n</jats:italic>
            <jats:sup>2.99</jats:sup>
            negative triangles in an edge-weighted graph.
          </jats:p>
          <jats:p>•Finding a minimum weight cycle in a graph of non-negative edge weights.</jats:p>
          <jats:p>•The replacement paths problem on weighted digraphs.</jats:p>
          <jats:p>•Finding the second shortest simple path between two nodes in a weighted digraph.</jats:p>
          <jats:p>•Checking whether a given matrix defines a metric.</jats:p>
          <jats:p>•Verifying the correctness of a matrix product over the (min, +)-semiring.</jats:p>
          <jats:p>•Finding a maximum subarray in a given matrix.</jats:p>
          <jats:p>
            Therefore, if APSP cannot be solved in
            <jats:italic>n</jats:italic>
            <jats:sup>3−ε</jats:sup>
            time for any ε > 0, then many other problems also need essentially cubic time. In fact, we show generic equivalences between matrix products over a large class of algebraic structures used in optimization, verifying a matrix product over the same structure, and corresponding triangle detection problems over the structure. These equivalences simplify prior work on subcubic algorithms for all-pairs path problems, since it now suffices to give appropriate subcubic triangle detection algorithms.
          </jats:p>
          <jats:p>Other consequences of our work are new combinatorial approaches to Boolean matrix multiplication over the (OR,AND)-semiring (abbreviated as BMM). We show that practical advances in triangle detection would imply practical BMM algorithms, among other results. Building on our techniques, we give two improved BMM algorithms: a derandomization of the combinatorial BMM algorithm of Bansal and Williams (FOCS’09), and an improved quantum algorithm for BMM.</jats:p>
title: Subcubic Equivalences Between Path, Matrix, and Triangle Problems
